home.title: See how your money habits add up
home.pitch: Arthik reads your bank or mobile-wallet transactions and gives you a financial health score from {lowest} to {highest}, with every point explained.
home.samples.note: Five invented people, each with six months of everyday transactions. Look at a few and you’ll see that the score measures habits, not income.
home.own.title: Your own transactions
home.own.text: Save a statement from your bank or mobile wallet as a CSV file, and Arthik will work out your score the same way.
home.privacy.lead: Your data stays in your browser.
home.privacy.text: Arthik runs entirely in your browser, so your file is never uploaded, and nothing is saved: refresh the page and it’s gone.
home.method.title: What goes into the score
home.method.note: Five measures of your money habits, each scored out of {highest}. Some count for more than others.
home.method.formulas: The score is worked out with published formulas, not by AI, so every point can be traced back to your own numbers.

sample.nusrat.kicker: Sample: Nusrat, university student in Dhaka
sample.nusrat.headline: Getting by, with little left over
sample.nusrat.summary: You live within your means, owe nothing and spend about the same every month, which is a solid base. What holds your score back is how little is left over: you keep {savedShare} of your income, and your emergency savings would cover about {bufferMonths} months of essentials. Eating out and delivery is the biggest of your wants.
sample.tanvir.kicker: Sample: Tanvir, freelance developer in Dhaka
sample.tanvir.headline: Saving well, but with big swings in spending
sample.tanvir.summary: Your pay arrives in dollars and changes from month to month, yet you keep {savedShare} of your income, put the same amount into a Deposit Pension Scheme (DPS) every month and owe nothing. What holds your score back most is uneven spending: buying a PlayStation made August your most expensive month. Wants take {wantsShare} of your spending, and your emergency savings would cover about {bufferMonths} months of essentials.
sample.farhana.kicker: Sample: Farhana, office worker in Dhaka
sample.farhana.headline: More going out than coming in
sample.farhana.summary: You earn nearly {incomeMultiple} times what Nusrat has coming in, yet your score is the lowest of all the sample people. Your loan and credit card payments take {debtShare} of your income, and once they are counted you pay out about {overspendShare} more than you earn. Loans from a relative have covered part of the gap, and you have almost no emergency savings. Your wants are a small share of your spending: what holds you back is how much of your pay goes on rent and debt.
sample.arif.kicker: Sample: Arif, MSc student in the UK
sample.arif.headline: Getting by abroad, with little to fall back on
sample.arif.summary: You live on part-time wages and money from your family, owe nothing and put a little aside every month. Even so, you keep only {savedShare} of your income, and your emergency savings would cover about {bufferMonths} months of essentials: those two are where you have the most to gain. Eating out and delivery is the biggest of your wants.
sample.rahim.kicker: Sample: Rahim, construction worker in Singapore
sample.rahim.headline: Sending money home, and still saving every month
sample.rahim.summary: Every month you send about {sentHomeShare} of your pay home, and your score is still the highest of all the sample people. Your spending hardly changes from month to month, you owe nothing, and you keep {savedShare} of your income. Emergency savings have the most room to grow: yours would cover about {bufferMonths} months of essentials.
sample.note: Summary written with Claude. The score itself comes from the formulas in <link>How the score works</link>.
sample.changed: You’ve changed some categories, so the written summary is hidden: it describes the transactions as they were.

howItWorks.title: How the score works
howItWorks.lead: Your score comes from fixed formulas applied to your own transactions, never from AI. The weights, anchor points and thresholds on this page are read from the same code that works out your score, so they always match what it does.
howItWorks.measures.title: The five measures
howItWorks.measures.intro: Your score is built from five measures of your money habits. Each gets its own score, from {lowest} to {highest}, and some count for more than others.
howItWorks.measures.anchors: Each measure’s score comes from the anchor points in its table. Between two anchor points, the score moves in a straight line: keeping {share} of your income, halfway between {from} and {to}, scores {score}. Beyond the first and last anchor points, the score stays the same.
howItWorks.savingsRate.detail: Spending is everything you paid out on essentials, wants, cash, other spending and anything uncategorised, less refunds. Money you put into savings isn’t spending, so it counts as kept. A rate below zero means you paid out more than you earned.
howItWorks.savingsRate.why: Keeping part of what you earn is what builds savings and carries you through a bad month. The more you keep, the higher the score.
howItWorks.savingsRate.notScored: Not scored if there’s no income in the months used, and then there’s no overall score either.
howItWorks.emergencySavings.formula: Emergency savings ÷ average monthly spending on essentials
howItWorks.emergencySavings.detail: Emergency savings are the savings you could use in an emergency. You enter the amount with your file, and each sample person comes with theirs. Spending on essentials is averaged over the months used.
howItWorks.emergencySavings.why: Savings you can reach quickly let you meet a sudden cost without borrowing. The more months of essentials they would cover, the higher the score.
howItWorks.emergencySavings.notScored: Not scored if you don’t enter your emergency savings, or if there’s no spending on essentials to measure them against.
howItWorks.debtPayments.detail: Debt payments are what you pay on loans, credit cards and buy-now-pay-later plans. Money you borrow is neither income nor spending, so it isn’t counted.
howItWorks.debtPayments.why: Debt payments are money already spoken for before the month begins. The bigger their share of your income, the less room you have, so the score falls as the share rises.
howItWorks.debtPayments.notScored: Not scored if there’s no income in the months used.
howItWorks.debtPayments.axis: Share of income on debt payments
howItWorks.needsWants.detail: Cash, other spending such as gifts, and anything uncategorised are left out, because they can’t be called needs or wants.
howItWorks.needsWants.why: Essentials are hard to cut. Wants are where you have room to adjust when money is tight, so the smaller their share, the higher the score. It isn’t a judgement of what you enjoy.
howItWorks.needsWants.notScored: Not scored if there’s no spending on essentials or wants.
howItWorks.stability.formula: Standard deviation of monthly spending ÷ average monthly spending
howItWorks.stability.detail: This is the coefficient of variation: roughly, how far a typical month strays from your average, as a share of that average. The standard deviation is worked out over the months used, dividing by the number of months.
howItWorks.stability.why: Steady spending is easier to plan for and less likely to run ahead of your income. The more your spending swings from month to month, the lower the score.
howItWorks.stability.notScored: {count, plural, one {Not scored with fewer than # complete month of data, or with no spending.} other {Not scored with fewer than # complete months of data, or with no spending.}}
howItWorks.points.title: How the points add up
howItWorks.points.round: Each measure’s score is rounded to a whole number.
howItWorks.points.multiply: Its points are that score times how much the measure counts. With all five measures scored, the points always come out exact to the hundredth.
howItWorks.points.total: The points are added up. The total, rounded to a whole number with halves rounded up, is your score.

howItWorks.example.intro: Here are made-up numbers for the five measures, worked through by the same code that works out your score.
howItWorks.example.result: The total, {total}, rounds to {score}, which is {band}.
howItWorks.reweight.title: When a measure can’t be scored
howItWorks.reweight.text: A measure that can’t be worked out is marked “Not scored”, with the reason. Its weight is shared among the other measures, in proportion to their own weights. Without emergency savings, the example above would count like this:
howItWorks.reweight.points: Shared-out weights are rounded when they’re shown. Points are still kept in hundredths: each measure’s points are rounded down, and any hundredths left over go one at a time to the measures that lost most in rounding, so the points always add up exactly to the total.
howItWorks.noScore.title: When there’s no score
howItWorks.noScore.intro: Your score isn’t shown in these cases:
howItWorks.noScore.noMonth: Your transactions don’t cover a single complete month.
howItWorks.noScore.noIncome: There’s no income in the months used. Savings rate and debt payments are both measured against income.
howItWorks.noScore.tooFew: Fewer than {min} of the {total} measures can be scored.
howItWorks.bands.title: The three bands
howItWorks.bands.intro: Your score falls in one of three bands. Each measure’s own score is placed in the same bands, so you can see which of your habits are strong and which need work.
howItWorks.months.title: Which months count
howItWorks.months.intro: Your score uses whole calendar months: the most recent complete ones in your data, up to {max}.
howItWorks.months.between: Every month between your first and last transaction counts.
howItWorks.months.first: The first month counts only if your transactions start by day {days} of it.
howItWorks.months.last: The last month counts only if they reach its final {days} days.
howItWorks.months.example: For example, transactions from {first} to {last} use {range}.
howItWorks.months.firstLeftOut: {month} is left out because they start after day {days}.
howItWorks.months.lastLeftOut: {month} is left out because they stop before its final {days} days.
howItWorks.months.shown: Your score page always says which months were used.
howItWorks.categories.title: How your transactions are sorted
howItWorks.categories.intro: Each transaction gets a category, matched from its description. You can change any category in the transactions table on your score page, and the score is worked out again. A category’s group decides how the score treats it.
howItWorks.group.other_spending.treatmen: Counts as spending, but as neither a need nor a want.
howItWorks.group.debt.treatment: Counts as debt payments. It isn’t spending.
howItWorks.group.savings.treatment: Isn’t spending: it’s money you keep, so it counts as saved.
howItWorks.group.cash.treatment: Counts as spending, because cash is assumed to be spent. It’s left out of needs vs. wants.
howItWorks.group.refund.treatment: Takes money off your spending. It isn’t income.
howItWorks.group.not_counted.treatment: Left out entirely, so money you move or borrow never looks like income or spending.
howItWorks.group.uncategorised.treatment: Counts as spending, but is left out of needs vs. wants.
howItWorks.category.savings_deposit: Savings deposit or Deposit Pension Scheme (DPS)
howItWorks.rules.cash.title: Cash withdrawals
howItWorks.rules.cash.text: Cash you take out, at an ATM or as a mobile-wallet cash-out, counts as spending, because cash is assumed to be spent. It’s left out of needs vs. wants, since there’s no telling what it bought. If your statement shows the cash-out charge on a line of its own, that goes under {fees}.
howItWorks.rules.refunds.title: Refunds
howItWorks.rules.refunds.text: A refund or reversal is taken off your total spending. It isn’t counted as income, and it isn’t taken off any one category.
howItWorks.rules.unrecognised.title: Money in that isn’t recognised
howItWorks.rules.unrecognised.text: Money in that matches nothing Arthik knows is counted as {otherIncome}, because most money arriving in a personal account is income or family support. Each one is flagged in your transactions table, so you can change it to a transfer or a loan if that’s what it was. Loans received, cash deposits and savings withdrawals are never counted as income: they belong to the {notCounted} group.
howItWorks.rules.accounts.title: Several accounts in one file
howItWorks.rules.accounts.text: One file can hold more than one account, such as your bank and your mobile wallet. Moving money between your own accounts goes under {ownTransfer}, which isn’t counted, so nothing is counted twice.
howItWorks.rules.card.title: Credit card bills
howItWorks.rules.card.text: Paying your credit card bill counts as a debt payment, even when you pay it in full. If your file also has the card’s own purchases, change the bill payment to {ownTransfer}. Otherwise the same spending is counted twice: once as purchases and again as a debt payment.
howItWorks.rules.family.title: Money sent to family
howItWorks.rules.family.text: {familyOut} counts as an essential, not a want. Supporting family is a core obligation for many households and for people working abroad, and the score doesn’t penalise it.
howItWorks.rules.currency.title: Other currencies
howItWorks.rules.currency.text: Amounts in other currencies are converted to taka before anything is worked out, at exchange rates from {source} as of {date}. The rates come bundled with Arthik, so nothing is fetched. Every measure is a ratio, so the currency you choose to view doesn’t change your score.
howItWorks.framework.title: Where the method comes from
howItWorks.framework.inspired: The score is inspired by the Financial Health Network’s FinHealth Score. That framework looks at four pillars of financial health, Spend, Save, Borrow and Plan, and places people in three bands. Arthik uses the same three bands.
howItWorks.framework.measured: The FinHealth Score is measured with a survey. Arthik works from transactions instead, which show how you spend, save and borrow. Planning can’t be seen in transactions, so Arthik doesn’t measure it.
howItWorks.limits.title: Limitations
howItWorks.limits.plan: Planning isn’t measured. It’s one of the FinHealth Score’s four pillars, but it can’t be seen in transactions.
howItWorks.limits.card: Credit card payments count as debt payments, even when you pay the bill in full.
howItWorks.limits.anchors: The anchor points are reasoned benchmarks. They weren’t fitted statistically to data about real people.
howItWorks.limits.stability: Spending stability looks at your spending, not at how steady your income is.
howItWorks.limits.file: The score sees only the accounts in your file. It can’t see cash you hold, money in other accounts, what you own or how much you owe in total.
howItWorks.limits.categories: Categories are matched from descriptions, and some may be wrong. It’s worth checking yours in the transactions table.
howItWorks.limits.savings: Emergency savings are taken from the figure you enter, which Arthik can’t check.
howItWorks.limits.rates: Exchange rates are one dated snapshot, not the rate on the day each payment was made.
howItWorks.privacy.title: Your privacy
howItWorks.privacy.browser: Your file is read and scored in your browser. It’s never uploaded.
howItWorks.privacy.nothingSaved: Nothing about your money is saved, not even on your device. Refresh the page and your file and any categories you changed are gone.
howItWorks.privacy.prefs: Arthik remembers only two things on this device: the language and the currency you chose.
howItWorks.privacy.noTracking: There are no cookies, no analytics and no tracking.
about.title: About Arthik
about.lead: Arthik turns your bank or mobile-wallet transactions into a financial health score, and shows how every point of it was worked out.
about.why.title: Why it was made
about.why.who: Arthik is made for people in Bangladesh and Bangladeshis living abroad. It reads mobile-wallet transactions as well as bank ones, works in taka unless you choose another currency, and counts money sent to family as an essential, not a want.
about.why.inclusion: The aim is financial inclusion: a clear, free check-up on your money habits that anyone can use, with no account to open.
about.why.habits: The score measures habits, not income. Among the sample people, {farhana} earns nearly {incomeMultiple} times what {nusrat} has coming in, yet scores lowest. {rahim} sends about {sentHomeShare} of his pay home every month and still scores highest.
about.who.title: Who made it
about.who.text: Arthik was made by Rubayet Rezwan. It was built with Claude Code.
about.ai.score: The score never comes from AI. It’s worked out in your browser, with the formulas set out in <link>How the score works</link>.
about.ai.summaries: The short summaries of the sample people were written with Claude. Every number in them is filled in from the same calculations as the score.
about.not.title: What Arthik is not
about.source.title: Source code
about.source.text: The code is on GitHub, including every formula and the tests that check it.
